description: Authorization that happened, and was about something else. Every handler here calls a real permission service and hands it the caller's identity, so the ownership policy's presumption -- `a helper receiving actor identity is presumed to enforce` -- is satisfied by all nine, and it was: this whole corpus read as clean before the relation was stated. What separates the three findings from the six clean routes is not whether a check ran but WHICH KEY it named. Three shapes are asserted, and each was a true finding on a production repository: the write reaches a record the check never mentioned (unleash's segment controller); a check sits between them and proves only that the row EXISTS, which every row does; and the row being written is the authorized one while a field being set names a different record, which is how a record gets re-parented onto something nobody checked (umami's report endpoint). The six clean routes are the shapes that make the rule usable rather than noisy -- the write keyed by the authorized key itself, a lookup carrying both keys, a comparison against the actor, a selection that carries both keys and needs no check above it, a permission that names no record at all, and a route with no identity anywhere. That last one produces a finding from the OTHER rule and the corpus asserts it, because a fixture that hid it would be asserting the absence of something that is there.

expected.note: authorized against the project in the route, keyed by a strategy id out of the body, and nothing asks whether that strategy is in that project
existence is not authorization: featureExists answers whether the row is there, which it always is, and mentions the authorized key not at all
the row being written IS the authorized one and the field being set names a different record; the depth the two identifiers sit at in the call is what tells this from a selection scoped by both keys

a different rule on a different route, and both are true: no identity reaches this handler at all, so there is no scope to compare against and the missing-ownership rule is the one with something to say
